<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The original Butler-Volmer (BV) relation \cite{DW20,RFR22,DV12} computes the exchange current density ${  i_{{ek}}^{\textrm{\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\tiny\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt BV}}  }$ per unit area $[Am^{-2}]$. Indeed, at the pore scale, the BV flux is given by a flux of charge across the interface between the electrode and the electrolyte. In a reduced one-dimensional model (the macroscopic average model), the volumetric current density ${  j_{{ek}}^{\textrm{\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\tiny\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt BV}}  }$ per unit volume $[Am^{-3}]$ is introduced as a source term in the species conservation equation by the macroscopic averaging (Volume of fluid (VOF) paradigm) used in a porous media system \cite{RBB12}. Consequently, in the literature, two current density versions coexist and may lead to some confusion in the applications. One has to carefully check whether the formulation uses a density current per unit area \cite{DW20} or per unit volume \cite{XNBD17}. \qedsymbol
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
For a discharging cell, ${  j_{{en}}^{\textrm{\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\tiny\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt BV}}  }>0$ and ${  j_{{ep}}^{\textrm{\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\tiny\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt BV}}  }<0$ means that we have the creation of electrons at the negative electrode, and the electrons are flowing from the anode towards the cathode with $I>0$. 
On the contrary, charging the cell means that ${  j_{{en}}^{\textrm{\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\tiny\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt BV}}  }<0$ and ${  j_{{ep}}^{\textrm{\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\tiny\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt BV}}  }>0$, we have a consumption of electrons at the negative electrode and $I<0$.\qedsymbol
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
When $\alpha_k=1/2$, we recover the hyperbolic sine function and the current density reads
$$
{  j_{{ek}}^{\textrm{\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\tiny\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt BV}}  }=2\,j^0_{ek}\,\sinh\big (f \eta_{ek}/2\big ). 
$$
For $\alpha\neq 1/2$ we define a new class of special functions ${\textrm{\rm bsinh}}(\eta,\beta)$ and ${\textrm{\rm bcosh}}(\eta,\beta)$, referred to here as $b$-hyperbolic trigonometry function, presented and studied in section \ref{sec::b-trigonometry}. \qedsymbol
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
The well-balanced relation between the creation and consumption of \ce{Li} is then given by
\begin{equation}\label{eq_conservation_BV}
L_n\ { {\overline \jmath}_{{en}}^{\textrm{\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\tiny\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt BV}}  }(t)+L_p\ { {\overline \jmath}_{{ep}}^{\textrm{\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\@setfontsize\tiny\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt\@vipt\@viipt BV}}  }(t)=0. \hskip3em \qedsymbol
\end{equation}
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
Note that the potential difference $\Delta_{elec}=\Phi_{cp}-\Phi_{cn}$ corresponds to the voltage between the anode and the cell cathode. \qedsymbol
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
Cancelling the time derivative does not mean that the problem is time-independent. We just say that the concentrations of the different species vary sufficiently slowly to consider that the term $\partial_t c_e$ is not significant with respect to the other contributions. However, the parameters, such as the source term, may still depend on time. \qedsymbol
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rem_I-linearity-boundary}
By construction, the average approximation functions ${{\widehat c}}_{en}(I)$, ${{\widehat c}}_{es}(I)$, ${{\widehat c}}_{ep}(I)$ together with the values at the interface with the collectors ${{\widehat c}}_{en,c}(I)$ and ${{\widehat c}}_{en,c}(I)$ are linear in terms of intensity $I$.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
For the particular case $\alpha_n= \alpha_p=1/2$, we recover the standard hyperbolic functions, and the relation reads
$$
g(I,R_{ext})=(R_{ext}+R_{int})I+\frac{2}{f} \left [ \arg\sinh\left ( \frac{I}{\iota_n}\right)+\arg\sinh\left ( \frac{I}{\iota_p}\right) \right ].
\hskip3em \qedsymbol
$$
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:existence_uniqueness}
For any $R_{ext}\geq 0$, there exists a unique intensity $\bar I$ such that  $V_{res}(\bar I,R_{ext})=0$.
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
Function $g(I,R_{ext})$ also depends on other parameters, such as the average concentrations. We do not mention it explicitly for the sake of simplicity, but when the concentration dependency would be critical, we overload the notation with $g(I_0,R_{ext};{{\overline c}}_n,{{\overline c}}_{en},{{\overline c}}_p,{{\overline c}}_{ep})$. \qedsymbol
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- defn-1: body_md -->
$I_{e}^+$ and $I_{e}^-$ are, respectively, the highest and lowest diffusion-limited current densities. They represent the bounds to which the intensity $I$ must belong to guarantee the physical eligibility of the concentration. Their values are closely connected to the diffusion coefficients $D_{ek}, k \in \{n,s,p\}$ and assess the capacity to transport the cation from one electrode to another. 
Such intensities are a strong limitation on the time required for charging and discharging the cell since they represent a physical limit to the intensity. \qedsymbol
<!-- end defn-1 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
Note that taking $I[k]=I_e^+$ or $I[k]=I_e^-$ is impossible, since we get a null concentration. Consequently, $\Delta_c[k]$ is not defined (the logarithmic function $\ln$ requires the argument to belong to $]0,+\infty[$). \qedsymbol
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- defn-2: body_md -->
Let $\beta\in [0,1]$, we define the b-hyperbolic sine and cosine functions with
$$
{\textrm{\rm bsinh}}(x,\beta)=\frac{\exp(2\beta x)-\exp(2(\beta-1)x)}{2},\quad
{\textrm{\rm bcosh}}(x,\beta)=\frac{\exp(2\beta x)+\exp(2(\beta-1)x)}{2}.
$$
Such function are well-defined, and differentiable on $\mathbb R$ and one has $\chi(\eta)=2\,{\textrm{\rm bsinh}}(\eta\,f/2;\beta)$.
<!-- end defn-2 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
We have the algebraic relations
$$
{\textrm{\rm bsinh}}(x,\beta)=\exp((2\beta-1)x)\sinh(x),\quad {\textrm{\rm bcosh}}(x,\beta)=\exp((2\beta-1)x)\cosh(x),
$$
$$
{\textrm{\rm bsinh}}(x,1-\beta)=-{\textrm{\rm bsinh}}(-x,\beta),\quad {\textrm{\rm bcosh}}(x,1-\beta)={\textrm{\rm bcosh}}(-x,\beta).
$$
Moreover, the derivatives read
\begin{eqnarray*}
{\textrm{\rm bsinh}}'(x,\beta)&=&(2\beta-1){\textrm{\rm bsinh}}(x,\beta)+{\textrm{\rm bcosh}}(x,\beta)\\
{\textrm{\rm bcosh}}'(x,\beta)&=&(2\beta-1){\textrm{\rm bcosh}}(x,\beta)+{\textrm{\rm bsinh}}(x,\beta)
\end{eqnarray*}
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
For any $\beta\in [0,1]$, the application $x\to y={\textrm{\rm bsinh}}(x,\beta)$ is a bijection from $\mathbb R$ onto $\mathbb R$ and we denote by $y\to x=\arg {\textrm{\rm bsinh}}(y,\beta)$ the inverse function.
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
The derivative reads
\begin{eqnarray*}
{\textrm{\rm bsinh}}'(x,\beta)&=&(2\beta-1){\textrm{\rm bsinh}}(x,\beta)+{\textrm{\rm bcosh}}(x,\beta)\\
                &=&\exp((2\beta-1) x)\Big [(2\beta-1)\sinh(x)+\cosh(x)\Big ]\\
                &=&\exp((2\beta-1) x)\Big [\beta \exp(x)+(1-\beta)\exp(-x)]
\end{eqnarray*}
Hence we have a convex combination of two positive functions and conclude that ${\textrm{\rm bsinh}}'(x,\beta)>0$ for all $x\in \mathbb R$.
Since ${\textrm{\rm bsinh}}(x,\beta)$ is a strictly increasing function from $\mathbb R$ onto $\mathbb R$, it admits an inverse function $y\to x={\textrm{\rm arg\,bsinh}}(y,\beta)$ from $\mathbb R$ onto $\mathbb R$, which is differentiable with strictly positive derivative.$\square$
<!-- end head-1 -->
